For this fintech workflow, the best choice is the one that can be integrated quickly without weakening expiry, abuse controls, delivery visibility, or rollback. A broad API surface is useful only if the first email remains boring to operate. Start with the /v1/email/send endpoint for the password-reset message, keep the reset token and its short expiry in the application, and maintain an explicit suppression-list check before sending. This keeps the security boundary in the service that owns the user session while leaving delivery to the email provider. items.title: Never Call an LLM From Your ERP: AI Middleware Architecture
items.summary: Your ERP just called an LLM synchronously. The model took 31 seconds. The ERP gave up at 30. Now 1,200 orders are stuck between "paid" and "shipped", and nobody knows which ones the AI already processed. AI Middleware Architecture The mistake is treating an LLM like a database call. It isn't one. It's slow, it's non-deterministic, and it fails in ways your ERP was never designed to handle. So you never connect them directly. You put a middleware layer in between, and that layer has one job: absorb the chaos. Step one: the ERP fires a webhook and gets an immediate response. 200 milliseconds, done. The ERP is free. Step two: the event lands in a queue. Not processed, queued. Now you control throughput, retries, and rate limits against the model provider. Step three: stateless workers pull jobs and call the model. They scale horizontally: two workers on a quiet Tuesday, 40 on Black Friday. Step four is the one most teams skip: validation. The model's answer is untrusted input. It gets parsed against a strict schema before it ever touches your ERP. If confidence is low, it goes to a human. Every decision gets written to an audit log. Confusing those meanings can leave a player showing video while the required verification resource never runs. This is especially relevant when a player moves from a browser test page to an app or another environment with a different JavaScript runtime. The same resource URL does not establish the same available APIs. VAST 4.3 section 3.17.1 provides the selection rules. The integration work is to apply them to a real environment, preserve the selected resource and verify what actually executed. A resource marked browserOptional="true" declares support for execution without DOM and other browser built-ins. The resource remains JavaScript. The flag does not replace it with a native measurement vendor SDK. For browser or webview execution, the specification prefers resources marked false when both forms are available. A non-browser JavaScript environment may execute only resources marked true. If it receives only unsuitable resources, the associated not-executed reporting must remain visible. items.title: Let your AI assistant draft customer replies (with a human in the loop): elozi-mcp
items.summary: I build Elozi, a customer-service workspace. I wanted AI assistants to help with support without giving them free rein, so I published elozi-mcp (MIT, v0.1.1). It is a small stdio bridge that connects desktop agents (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP stdio client) to Elozi's hosted endpoint. It stores no data locally, adds no telemetry and does not retry tool calls automatically. Permissions come from the token. In the Elozi panel you create an agent of type "Agent via MCP" and a service identity with channels, departments, capabilities, validity and daily quotas. The assistant only sees tools your token allows. A good start is conversation.read plus reply.submit: it reads and drafts, a person approves. Add reply.send or conversation.manage only when you want it to act alone. Requirements: Node.js 22+ and an ELOZI_API_TOKEN (starts with elozi_svc_, shown once). items.title: Usestate in Reactjs
items.summary: Usestate UseState is one of the React Hooks used to manage state in a component. Normally, when we use a local variable, changing its value does not trigger a re-render of the component. But useState allows us to store a value and update the UI whenever that value changes. Using a normal variable doesn't trigger a re-render the UI still doesn't show anything about your process by using a normal variable. To overcome this using usestate updates changes in UI everytime when the component gets re-rendered. const [stateVariable, stateFunction] = useState(0); Statevariable -It stored the current state value. StateFunction - It is a setterfunction used to update the current state value. When called, it tells React to re-render the component so the UI can reflect the updated state.

items.title: How to Build an Express Middleware Setup for Error Tracking: 2026 Property Costs
items.summary: Short answer: use one Express error-tracking middleware setup that emits a normalized JSON event with run_id, property_id, stage, and error_code; retain the compact event longer than its raw payload so nightly property-pipeline costs can be attributed without storing every request body. A nightly property-management pipeline usually does not need a bigger error platform. It needs one error record that answers three questions: which run failed, which property or tenant cohort was affected, and what retention decision created the bill. Put that context into structured logs at the Express boundary, propagate a request or job identifier, and keep verbose payloads on a short retention schedule. The least complex useful implementation is an error-handling middleware that emits one normalized event per failed request, while the pipeline worker emits the same shape for scheduled jobs. The middleware should preserve the original error for local diagnostics, remove secrets before serialization, and let the process-level policy decide whether the request can continue. items.title: Run TypeScript in Node.js Without a Build Step: Type Stripping Tested on Node 22, 24 and 26
items.summary: Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com. You can now run a .ts file with plain node app.ts, no tsx, no ts-node, no build step. Type stripping has been on by default since Node.js 22.18.0 and 23.6.0, and it became stable in Node.js 24.12.0 and 25.2.0. On Node.js 26 LTS it is simply how Node works. But "Node runs TypeScript" has sharp edges. Enums fail. Parameter properties fail. Decorators fail. Imports without .ts fail. And Node never checks your types. I tested every one of these on Node.js 22.20.0, 24.22.2 and 26.13.0, and this post shows the exact errors, the tsconfig.json that catches all of them before runtime, and how startup time compares to tsx and precompiled JavaScript. Node replaces TypeScript type annotations with whitespace and runs what is left as JavaScript. It does not type-check, it ignores tsconfig.json, and it only accepts erasable syntax: TypeScript that disappears completely when you delete the types. From the Node.js TypeScript docs history table: Node.js version Change v22.6.0 Type stripping added behind --experimental-strip-types v23.6.0, v22.18.0 Enabled by default v24.3.0, v22.18.0 No more experimental warning v24.

items.title: React Hook: useContext
items.summary: useContext is used to avoid the props drilling in react. If you send this initDataUnsafe user ID directly to your API to look up accounts, process orders, or issue rewards, your application is completely vulnerable to identity spoofing. Because Mini Apps are standard web applications running inside an embedded browser frame, anyone can open your Mini App's URL in a standard desktop browser, open Developer Tools, and mutate window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe to contain any target user ID. An attacker can easily impersonate administrators or drain balances belonging to other users. items.title: useEffect in React
items.summary: 1. What Is useEffect? useEffect is a React Hook used to handle side effects in functional components. A side effect is an operation that happens outside the normal process of displaying the UI. Some common examples are: Fetching data from an API. Setting a timer. Updating the document title. Adding event listeners. Subscribing to external services. First, we need to import useEffect from React. import { useEffect } from "react"; useEffect(() => { // Side effect code }, []); Here: The first argument is a callback function containing the side effect. The second argument is the dependency array. If we don't provide a dependency array, the effect runs after every render. import { useEffect, useState } from "react"; function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); useEffect(() => { console.log("Component rendered"); }); return ( {count} setCount(count + 1)}> Increase ); } export default Counter; Every time the component renders, the effect runs. items.title: React Props: How Do Components Share Data With Each Other?
items.summary: Imagine you're building an e-commerce application. You have one Product component, but you need to display different products: Laptop – ₹50,000 Mobile – ₹20,000 Headphones – ₹2,000 Would you create three separate components for these products? Not necessary! React provides something called Props (Properties) that allows you to reuse the same component with different data. 1. What are Props? Props are a way to pass data from a parent component to a child component. Think of a component as a function. Props act like the function's parameters. Let's understand with an example. Parent Component function App() { return ( ); } Here, we're passing different values to the same Product component. Child Component function Product(props) { return ( {props.name} Price: ₹{props.price} ); } The child component receives the values through the props object. Output Laptop Price: ₹50000 Mobile Price: ₹20000 Headphones Price: ₹2000 Notice something? We created only one component but reused it three times with different data. That's the power of props! 2. items.title: Modeling Cash Drawer Variance: Event-Sourced Shifts in an Offline POS
items.summary: The payments side of our POS (StoreFlux, a headless commerce backend) got most of the write-up attention so far. The shift and cash-drawer accounting underneath it is smaller in scope but had its own interesting constraints, so here's how that part actually works. A cashier opens a shift with a starting cash count. Through the shift they take cash payments, maybe pay cash out for something (a supplier delivery, petty expenses), maybe put more cash in. At close, they count the drawer again. The number that matters is: what should be in there, given everything that happened, versus what's actually in there. That gap is the variance, and it has to be a real computed number a manager can look at, not something eyeballed. Everything at the register already flows through an outbox of client-generated, idempotent events (sales, refunds, product edits — covered in an earlier post). Shifts fit the same model instead of getting special-cased: shift.opened (carries the starting float), cash.moved (a paid-in or paid-out, with a reason), and shift.closed (carries the counted-at-close amount). items.title: Privacy Boundaries for AI Telemetry
items.summary: Turning off prompt capture is not enough to enforce a complete telemetry recording policy. Exceptions can still include customer text in spans. If an investigation is limited to ten samples, it can end up with forty if four replicas each track their own counters. Queued samples can exceed their intended retention if the destination resets the expiry upon arrival. The recording-policy tip establishes what to allow. This article focuses on enforcement: inspect the actual SDK output, authorize capture with a narrow scope, reserve quota across replicas, and carry an absolute expiry through every copy of evidence. The example is a support assistant that reads a private ticket, fetches a refund policy, calls an eligibility tool, and drafts a reply. An investigation requires the policy excerpt and the generated reply, but should not collect the ticket or account-tool payload. Keep ordinary message capture explicitly disabled. [...] Those leaving Canva will receive at least six months of salary and retain healthcare coverage for a further 12 months in countries where workers receive that benefit. They can also keep their laptops. Those leaving can also apply for US$10,000 (A$14,000) grants to start their own ventures. items.title: Opening a panel right under the text caret on macOS
items.summary: I'm building yabbistir, a clipboard history for macOS. Its one trick is where it opens: press ⇧⌘V and the panel appears 8 points under the text caret of whatever app you're typing in. You type to search, press ↵, and the item is pasted back into that app. Your eyes don't travel and your hands don't leave the keyboard. That needs three things macOS doesn't hand you directly: the caret's position in someone else's app, a sensible answer when that app won't tell you, a window that takes keystrokes without taking focus away from the app you're typing in. Here is how each one works, with code from the app, shortened. There's no "where is the caret" API on macOS. There is the Accessibility API, the one assistive apps like VoiceOver use to read other apps' interfaces. Your app needs the Accessibility permission for it (AXIsProcessTrusted() tells you whether you have it), and then it can ask three questions: Which element has keyboard focus? items.title: Deadlocks γιατί εμφανίζονται και πώς τα μειώνουμε
items.summary: Μια συναλλαγή μπορεί να προστατεύει προσωρινά δεδομένα από ασύμβατες ενέργειες άλλων συναλλαγών. Αυτή η προστασία ονομάζεται κλείδωμα — lock. Αν μια άλλη εργασία χρειάζεται τα ίδια δεδομένα, μπορεί να περιμένει. Η απλή αναμονή μπορεί να εξελιχθεί φυσιολογικά: Η A κρατά μια γραμμή. Η B περιμένει. Η A ολοκληρώνεται. Η B συνεχίζει. Αυτό λέγεται blocking. Σε ένα deadlock, η αναμονή γίνεται κύκλος: Η A κρατά τη γραμμή 1 και περιμένει τη γραμμή 2. Η B κρατά τη γραμμή 2 και περιμένει τη γραμμή 1. Καμία δεν μπορεί να συνεχίσει χωρίς παρέμβαση. Ο SQL Server επιλέγει μια συναλλαγή, την ακυρώνει με rollback και επιστρέφει το σφάλμα 1205. Η άλλη μπορεί πλέον να συνεχίσει. Τεκμηρίωση Microsoft Έστω ότι δύο εργασίες ενημερώνουν τους ίδιους δύο μετρητές. Αν η μία ξεκινά από τον μετρητή 1 και η άλλη από τον 2, μπορεί να σχηματιστεί ο προηγούμενος κύκλος. Χρησιμοποιούμε την ίδια σειρά και στις δύο: BEGIN TRANSACTION; UPDATE Counters SET Value = Value + 1 WHERE Id = 1; UPDATE Counters SET Value = Value + 1 WHERE Id = 2; COMMIT; Έτσι αφαιρούμε τη συγκεκριμένη αιτία του deadlock. Χρειαζόμαστε για το τι επιτρέπεται να διαβάσει η αγορά και πότε κάποια εργασία πρέπει να περιμένει. Αυτούς τους κανόνες επιλέγουμε μέσω του επιπέδου απομόνωσης — isolation level. Τα παρακάτω αφορούν SQL Server. Διαβάζουμε αλλαγές άλλων συναλλαγών μόνο αφού οριστικοποιηθούν, δηλαδή αφού γίνει commit. Μπορούμε να διαβάσουμε αλλαγές πριν οριστικοποιηθούν. Παράδειγμα: βλέπουμε προσωρινή τιμή 80€, αλλά ο διαχειριστής ακυρώνει την αλλαγή με rollback. Η τιμή παραμένει 100€. But letting an agent execute every action automatically isn't always a good idea. Consider a finance assistant that can prepare payment requests. It receives a request to transfer $15,000 to a supplier, understands it, finds the payment tool, and prepares the operation. Should the application run that payment immediately? For low-risk operations, maybe. For sensitive or high-impact ones, a human should review the proposed action first. That's the idea behind human-in-the-loop AI agents in .NET: a controlled approval step between the agent's decision and the execution of a sensitive operation. items.title: NASA's Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth
items.summary: joshuark shares a report from Wired: After 22 years in orbit and a failed rescue mission this summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft -- which is roughly as big as a large elevator -- will fall. Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low. The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about the evolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and the destruction of stars by black holes. However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth's atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Without a propulsion system capable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered. The U.S. Space Force now expects Swift to reenter Earth's atmosphere around November 6. items.title: Cleaning duplicate photos inside Lightroom Classic and Capture One catalogs without breaking them
items.summary: Disclosure: I'm the developer of Folio Refresh, the Mac app this post is about. Most duplicate photo finders work on folders. Point them at a drive, they hash files, they move copies to the Trash. That is fine until the photos live in a Lightroom Classic or Capture One catalog. Delete a file behind Lightroom's back and the catalog shows a missing-photo badge; delete the wrong copy and you lose the edits, ratings and collections attached to it. When I built Folio Refresh I wanted it to clean duplicates inside those catalogs, so here is how it does that without corrupting them. A Lightroom Classic catalog (.lrcat) is a SQLite database. A Capture One catalog (.cocatalog) is a package with a SQLite database (.cocatalogdb) inside. Neither schema is documented, and both change between versions. That shapes every rule below. Scanning only ever opens the catalog read-only. Lightroom: SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY. SQLite guarantees a read-only connection cannot write the database or its log, so this is safe even while Lightroom has the catalog open; it is just another reader. items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

items.title: Dinosaur Blood Found In Fossils For the First Time
items.summary: Researchers have confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside the 115-million-year-old fossilized bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali from Brazil. The discovery challenges assumptions about how long blood-related biomolecules can survive and could help scientists study dinosaur metabolism, blood evolution and even how traces of ancient life might be preserved on other worlds. Popular Science reports: The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger. After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. items.title: Why your Mac stays awake after you close the lid: two sleep traps
items.summary: I make Vigil, a Mac app that keeps the machine awake for long jobs, even with the lid closed. Most of the work turned out to be the opposite problem: getting the Mac to sleep again afterward. Here are two traps I measured, and the commands to check your own Mac. Vigil holds the Mac awake with pmset disablesleep 1 and lets go with disablesleep 0. On 4 Sep I tested it on an M4 MacBook Air. I closed the lid at 20:27 and the hold ended at 20:42. At 22:50 the Mac was still awake, and hot, in a bag. pmset -g explained it: sleep 1 (sleep prevented by Claude, coreaudiod, powerd, sharingd, Sada) Lid-close sleep is a one-time event at the moment the lid closes. If something blocks it then, macOS doesn’t try again when the block lifts. All that’s left is idle sleep, and any app holding an idle assertion stops that too. The fix: when a hold ends while the lid is closed (AppleClamshellState is true), run pmset sleepnow as root right after disablesleep 0. Skip it if an external display is connected, because that person is using clamshell mode on purpose. .userInitiated quietly blocks sleep Sada, another of my apps, sat in that list above. items.title: Building a Private Photo Vault App for iPhone with No Account
items.summary: I build iPhone apps on my own. Secure Folder is the one I made for photos and videos I don't want in the camera roll. The vault stays on the phone. You don't sign up, and the photos aren't uploaded. The app doesn't use iCloud. I didn't want a login in front of a private photo. If the pictures lived on a server, someone could ask me to hand them over. The first launch is a 6-digit PIN for the vault. It isn't the iPhone passcode, so that passcode won't open these photos. Face ID or Touch ID can open the vault too, if you turn that on. The switch is in the Security tab. Auto-Lock is on by default, and it's one switch. There's no timer and no lock button. When the app leaves the screen, it locks. Coming back means the PIN, or Face ID if you turned that on. iOS keeps a picture of your app for the app switcher. If the cover waited until the app was fully in the background, that picture could be the last photo you had open. The blur goes up as soon as the app is no longer in the foreground. The lock follows when iOS has actually moved the app to the background. You can't turn the blur off, so the app switcher doesn't keep the last photo. People say "hide" and mean the file moved. items.title: Democrats Take Control of US Congress As Voters Reject Trump's Republicans
items.summary: Tuesday, November 3, was Election Day in the United States, and the results are (mostly) in: Democrats are projected to win control of both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms. The blue wave turned out to be more of a blue tsunami, ending Republican control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's second term. Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats in the 2026 midterms, including surprise victories in traditionally Republican strongholds such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. Kansas elected its first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 100 years (94 years to be exact), while Texas and South Carolina sent Democrats to the Senate for the first time in decades. Democrats also picked up seats in Ohio, Iowa, Maine, and North Carolina. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Shipping 130,000 WKContentRuleList rules without slowing down app launch
items.summary: I build Kipzy, an iPhone browser with a built-in ad blocker. The blocker uses EasyList and EasyPrivacy, which works out to about 130,000 WebKit content blocking rules. This post covers how Kipzy gets those rules into every WKWebView without hurting launch time and without recompiling when a user turns blocking off for one site. All numbers below come from the real lists. The compile times were measured on an M3 Pro Mac, which uses the same content blocker engine as iOS. An iPhone is slower. WKContentRuleListStore.compileContentRuleList turns a JSON rule list into WebKit's compiled bytecode. It's fast for a few hundred rules. Kipzy's 7 lists add up to about 18 MB of JSON, and compiling them takes this long: network-1 30000 rules 1.03s network-2 30000 rules 0.88s network-3 30000 rules 0.95s network-4 30000 rules 0.80s network-5 3753 rules 0.27s cosmetic-generic 757 rules 0.05s cosmetic-sites 5292 rules 0.54s That's about 4.5 seconds on a laptop chip. If any of it happens at launch, or on the main thread, the app feels broken. Compiled lists persist on disk. items.title: Action Runner iOS Architecture
items.summary: Around mid-2021, I'd started developing SwiftUI apps in a new way. I'd previously considered architectures like MVC, MVVM, VIPER, etc and many of them never felt right. I often found myself spending time considering where to put business logic. With SwiftUI, it wasn't entirely clear where data-level changes should be taking place. Most (or any?) business logic certainly shouldn't be living in the views, but should I be building controllers to manage data? When I did that, I ended up struggling to define the boundaries of each controller. Dependencies would start to get messy, and I'd start getting circular dependencies across controllers that called each other. Controllers would start to get really big, especially for authentication, and I'd often struggle to quickly find code I was looking for. Action? In my work using React, the one-way data flow in Redux and how it handled actions was an idea that came to mind to try to tame these large controllers I was noticing in my projects. But there is a catch: Schools that choose to restrict A.I. entirely will also lose access to Google search. A.I. features are now a standard part of Google's commercially available search engine. "Search and A.I. are deeply integrated," said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. If a school has banned A.I., he added, students "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available." items.summary: Swarms are AI systems where multiple agents cooperate towards a shared goal. This post discusses a technique called collective inference-time scaling, where agents scale the amount of useful work performed in parallel and the communication needed to achieve it. It also explains how to design incentives for parallel work, and covers the general topic of designing incentives for reinforcement learning.

items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)

Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

items.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI (31 minute read)
items.summary: OpenAI's monorepo's size and demands increased at a staggering pace over the last year, necessitating a revamp of the AI lab's source control system. Its technical staff built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches and to maximize read throughput. The team implemented the backend without interrupting any engineering work or changing how the team uses Git. Pando cut median push latency in production by nearly 5x, and it now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

The transition to Rust improved efficiency and highlighted the importance of clear testing, boundary setting, and human oversight in the development process.

We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. items.title: The surprising leadership dynamics in agent swarms (17 minute read)
items.summary: Agent swarms are groups of agents that work together to accomplish a task. Researchers created an experiment in which eight agents from four different models worked together to resolve simulated outages to understand how agents organize themselves in a swarm without a designated leader. They discovered two factors that could influence an agent's potential leadership: the agent's underlying models, and the order in which their name was listed in a prompt. This suggests that even seemingly minor details in how an agent swarm is configured can affect how agents coordinate.

items.title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?

He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen. But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop. items.title: Knowing How Is Not Knowing What (14 minute read)
items.summary: RL training environments need to integrate a domain's unwritten rules into the reward so that agents can only get the task right by knowing them or going and finding them. Environments should be built as one world exposed through several surfaces. This allows you to pose the same task at different difficulties by changing the surface, and agents get a chance to learn when to switch. The reward also reads the world, so agents that go through different surfaces get the same outcome score if they reach the same authorized result.

items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...

items.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
items.summary: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. Continue reading...
